etymology: From Old French doble, from Latin duplus, twofold. Webster 1828: twofold; twice as much; also, deceitful, acting two parts. In the Authorized Version the word runs along two tracks that never quite meet — double as the measure of inheritance, honour and recompense, and double as the mark of a divided man.
biblical_def: Double in Scripture is first a legal measure. The firstborn receives a double portion of all that he hath: for he is the beginning of his strength (Deuteronomy 21:17) — not twice each brother’s share as sentiment, but the inheritance right of the son who carries the family forward. Elisha asks for exactly that: let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me (2 Kings 2:9). He is not requesting twice Elijah’s power; he is asking to be treated as the prophetic firstborn, the heir of the office. Paul carries the measure into the church: Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine (1 Timothy 5:17). Double is also the measure of God’s dealings at both ends. In mercy, Isaiah’s Jerusalem hath received of the LORD'S hand double for all her sins (Isaiah 40:2), and in judgment, Babylon is told double unto her double according to her works (Revelation 18:6). But the second track is moral, and it is a warning: A double minded man is unstable in all his ways (James 1:8). The same word that names a doubled blessing names a doubled heart, and Scripture treats the second as a disease.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DOUBLE as twofold; twice as much; consisting of two of a sort together; and, of persons, deceitful, acting two parts, one openly and the other in secret. Webster gives both the arithmetical and the moral sense.
webster_full: DOUBLE, a. [L. duplus.] — Twofold; of two kinds. Twice as much; containing the same quantity or length repeated. Two of a sort together; coupled. Deceitful; acting two parts, one openly, the other in secret; as a double heart.

Webster’s final sense is James’s. The English word carries the moral meaning natively — a double dealer, a double tongue — and Scripture exploits it. To be doubled in portion is blessing; to be doubled in heart is instability, because a man with two centres has none.
scriptures: 2 Kings 2:9

And it came to pass, when they were gone over, that Elijah said unto Elisha, Ask what I shall do for thee, before I be taken away from thee. And Elisha said, I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me.
Deuteronomy 21:17
But he shall acknowledge the son of the hated for the firstborn, by giving him a double portion of all that he hath: for he is the beginning of his strength; the right of the firstborn is his.
1 Timothy 5:17
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
Isaiah 40:2
Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned: for she hath received of the LORD'S hand double for all her sins.
James 1:8
A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.
corruption_summary: Double is corrupted chiefly at 2 Kings 2:9, where Elisha’s request for the firstborn’s portion is read as a request for twice Elijah’s power — a misreading that has become the standing proof-text for seeking escalating anointings.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular reading of Elisha’s request makes it an ambition for greater power than his master’s, and it is then preached as a model: ask God for a double portion, expect more than those who went before. Deuteronomy 21:17 rules this out. The double portion is a fixed legal term for the inheritance of the firstborn, and Elisha, who has just been told to ask before Elijah is taken, is asking to be recognized as the prophetic heir. That is why he asks for a hard thing and why the sign given is whether he sees Elijah taken up. The request is for succession, not for escalation. Read as escalation, the verse becomes a warrant for the modern pursuit of ever-greater anointings, impartations, and transferable mantles — a pattern the New Apostolic Reformation has built on and which the closed canon and the cessation of the prophetic office forbid.

The second corruption is quieter and touches 1 Timothy 5:17. Double honour for elders who rule well has been read either as a bare command to pay ministers more, or, in reaction, as merely a call for greater respect. The context settles it: the next verse quotes Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn and The labourer is worthy of his reward, so material support is genuinely in view. But the word is honour, and the measure is ruling well and labouring in the word and doctrine. It is neither a salary scale nor a courtesy. It is a congregation’s duty to weight its regard, and its purse, toward faithful teaching — which is also why the surrounding verses immediately regulate how accusations against an elder are received.
roots_summary: The Hebrew word for double is the ordinary word for second or a copy, which is why it can mean an inheritance share, a repetition, or a duplicate. The Greek in James is a compound of two and soul, and it describes a man with two centres.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishneh (H4932) — second, double, a copy; used of the firstborn’s portion (Deuteronomy 21:17) and of the king’s copy of the law.
Greek diplous (G1362) — double, twofold (1 Timothy 5:17, double honour; Revelation 18:6).
Greek dipsuchos — two-souled, double-minded (James 1:8). Not a doubled blessing but a divided man. Untagged in this lexicon.
Greek dis (G1364) — twice, again; the numeral underlying the whole family, and the reason double can mean either repetition or duplicity.
usage: A double portion is the firstborn’s legal right (Deuteronomy 21:17); Elisha asks for succession, not for twice Elijah’s power.
Double honour (1 Timothy 5:17) is weighted regard and material support, measured by ruling well and labouring in the word.
A double minded man is unstable in all his ways (James 1:8) — doubled portion is blessing; doubled heart is disease.

etymology: Old English læst, superlative of læssa, less. Webster 1828: smallest; little beyond others, either in size, degree, quantity or dignity. In the Authorized Version least is a kingdom word: it marks where God characteristically starts, and it is the self-description of the men He used most.
biblical_def: Least in Scripture is rarely a measurement and almost always a verdict — and the verdict is regularly reversed. Gideon protests that his family is poor and he the least in his father’s house; Saul answers Samuel, Am not I a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? (1 Samuel 9:21). The Lord makes the pattern a principle: he that is least among you all, the same shall be great (Luke 9:48), and He measures the kingdom’s smallest member against the greatest man born of women — he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he (Matthew 11:11). The mustard seed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs (Matthew 13:32). Faithfulness is tested at the same scale: He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much (Luke 16:10), and the commandments are guarded there too, for whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches men so shall be called the least in the kingdom (Matthew 5:19). Paul, who had every credential, ends where the pattern ends: I am the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9), and later, less than the least of all saints (Ephesians 3:8). That is not affectation. It is what grace does to a man’s arithmetic.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LEAST as smallest; little beyond others, either in size, quantity, degree or dignity; the superlative of little. As an adverb, in the smallest or lowest degree.
webster_full: LEAST, a. [superl. of little.] — Smallest; little beyond others, either in size, quantity, degree or dignity; as the least insect; the least mercy. LEAST, adv. — In the smallest or lowest degree; in a degree below all others; as, to reward those who least deserve it.

Webster includes dignity among the things a man may be least in, and that is the biblical use. Scripture’s least is usually a ranking rather than a size — the smallest tribe, the youngest son, the last apostle — which is exactly what makes the reversals so pointed.
scriptures: Ephesians 3:8
Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ;
Matthew 25:40
And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
Luke 16:10
He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
Matthew 5:19

Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: but whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.
1 Corinthians 15:9
For I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.
corruption_summary: Least is corrupted most often at Matthew 25:40, where the least of these my brethren is detached from the brethren Christ names and made a general warrant for humanitarian activity, and at Matthew 5:19, where least commandments is used to grade God’s law into optional and essential tiers.
corruption_paragraphs: The least of these my brethren has become one of the most quoted and least examined phrases in Scripture. In the judgment scene the King identifies a specific group — His brethren, hungry, thirsty, strangers, naked, sick, and in prison — and the nations are judged by their treatment of them. The immediate reference is to Christ’s own people, and the passage is about how the world receives those who bear His name and His message. That reading does not cancel the church’s duty to the poor; Scripture commands mercy to the stranger, the widow, the orphan, and the afflicted in a hundred places, and the Christian who feeds the hungry is obeying God. But when Matthew 25 is made the charter for a general social programme, two things quietly follow: the works are severed from faith in Christ and made the ground of acceptance, and the church’s particular obligation to persecuted believers is diluted into everyone’s obligation to everyone. The verse is stronger, not weaker, when read as it stands.

Matthew 5:19 suffers the opposite handling. These least commandments is read as Christ’s own concession that some commands are minor and may be quietly retired — an assumption that then does considerable work in setting aside whatever a given age finds inconvenient, particularly on sexual order and creational design. But the verse is a warning, not a permission slip: the one who breaks the least commandment and teaches men so shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven. The Lord is defending the smallest jot and tittle in the very sentence, having just said He came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it. That some commandments are weightier is His own teaching elsewhere; that any are dispensable is precisely what He denies here.
roots_summary: Two Greek superlatives and one Hebrew adjective carry least. The Greek pair distinguishes the absolutely smallest from the merely small, and Paul coins a comparative on the superlative itself in Ephesians 3:8 — a grammatical impossibility used on purpose.
roots_lines: Greek elachistos (G1646) — smallest, least, most insignificant (Matthew 25:40; Luke 16:10; 1 Corinthians 15:9).
Greek mikros (G3398) — small, little, least; the ordinary word for size, and the root of English micro-.
Hebrew qātān (H6996) — small, young, insignificant, least (1 Samuel 9:21, Saul on his own family and tribe).
In Ephesians 3:8 Paul writes a comparative built on a superlative — less than the least, literally leaster. The grammar breaks because the point does.
usage: He that is least among you all, the same shall be great (Luke 9:48) — the kingdom’s ranking runs backwards from the world’s.
Faithful in that which is least (Luke 16:10): the small scale is where fidelity is actually tested.
Paul moves from the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9) to less than the least of all saints (Ephesians 3:8) — the direction of a man under grace.

etymology: Old English nacod, bare, unclothed. Webster 1828: not covered; bare; having no clothes on; also, open to view, manifest, unarmed, destitute. In the Authorized Version naked is the condition sin produced in Eden and the condition every man will be in before God unless he is clothed by Another.
biblical_def: Naked is the Bible’s word for exposure, and it enters Scripture at the fall. Before sin the man and his wife were naked and not ashamed; after it, the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons (Genesis 3:7). Nakedness itself did not change — their standing did. The first human industry was the manufacture of a covering, and God replaced it with coats of skins, which required a death. From there the word carries the whole doctrine. Job strips the question to its frame: Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither (Job 1:21). Nothing is carried in and nothing out. Hebrews applies it to the reader now rather than later: all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do (Hebrews 4:13). And the risen Christ diagnoses a wealthy congregation with the word they would least expect — thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked (Revelation 3:17) — and offers white raiment to buy from Him. The pattern never varies: man notices his nakedness, man sews something, God provides the covering. Fig leaves are the whole history of self-righteousness in one verse.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NAKED as not covered; bare; having no clothes on; open to view, not concealed, manifest; unarmed, defenceless; destitute of means of defence or support; also, plain, evident, undisguised.
webster_full: NAKED, a. [Sax. nacod.] — Not covered; bare; having no clothes on. Unarmed; defenceless; open; exposed; subject to. Open to view; not concealed; manifest. Destitute of means of defence or support. Plain; evident; undisguised; as the naked truth.

Every one of Webster’s senses is used somewhere in Scripture, and they converge on Hebrews 4:13 — all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him. There the word is simultaneously uncovered, defenceless, manifest, and undisguised. The English idiom the naked truth is the same figure, and it is the reason the word can name both the sinner’s shame and God’s sight of it.
scriptures: Genesis 3:7
And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.
Job 1:21
And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
Hebrews 4:13
Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.
Revelation 3:17
Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:
Revelation 16:15
Behold, I come as a thief. Blessed is he that watcheth, and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked, and they see his shame.
corruption_summary: Naked is corrupted when the shame that entered at the fall is treated as the real problem — a false modesty to be unlearned — rather than as the true signal of a real guilt, so that the remedy becomes self-acceptance instead of a covering God provides.
corruption_paragraphs: A now-standard account reads Genesis 3 as the origin of an unhealthy shame about the body, and prescribes the removal of the shame. Scripture prescribes the removal of the guilt. Adam and Eve were naked before the fall and unashamed; the body did not change, the standing did. Their shame was accurate — it was the conscience reporting a real breach — and God did not correct the diagnosis. He accepted it and answered it, replacing the fig leaves with coats of skins, which required the death of an animal and taught in one act that acceptable covering is provided, substitutionary, and costly. Any counsel that treats the shame as the disease leaves the guilt untouched and the man still uncovered, and it must ignore what God actually did in the garden.

The second corruption is the church’s own, and Revelation 3 names it. A congregation may be prosperous, active, and entirely satisfied — I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing — and be described by Christ as naked. Self-assessment is not the instrument by which spiritual condition is measured, which is why Hebrews 4:13 puts the reader under a gaze rather than in front of a mirror. The Laodicean remedy is instructive: they are counselled to buy white raiment of Him. Not to work on their self-perception, and not to sew. The only covering Scripture recognizes is the imputed righteousness of Christ, received by faith, and the fig leaf is what men make when they would rather manufacture a covering than receive one.
roots_summary: The Hebrew and Greek words for naked are plain and physical, and Scripture’s theology comes from where it places them — at the fall, at the grave, and before the throne. The Greek of Hebrews 4:13 adds a second image the English keeps: laid bare, with the neck exposed.
roots_lines: Hebrew ārōm — naked, bare (Genesis 3:7; Job 1:21). Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.
Greek gumnos — naked, unclothed, poorly clad (Hebrews 4:13; Revelation 3:17; Revelation 16:15). The root of English gymnasium. Untagged in this lexicon.
Hebrew bōsh — to be ashamed, to be confounded; the companion word from Genesis 2:25 onward, joining nakedness to shame from the start. Untagged in this lexicon.
The second word in Hebrews 4:13, rendered opened, carries the sense of a neck bent back and exposed — the posture of a sacrifice under the knife.
usage: They knew that they were naked and sewed fig leaves (Genesis 3:7) — the first human industry was the manufacture of a covering.
Naked came I out of my mother's womb (Job 1:21): nothing is carried in, and nothing out.
Laodicea was rich and naked at the same time (Revelation 3:17); self-assessment does not measure the soul’s condition.

etymology: Old English heard, firm, severe, strong. Webster 1828: firm; solid; compact; not easily penetrated; difficult; oppressive; and, of the heart, unfeeling, obdurate. In the Authorized Version the word runs three ways — what is difficult, what is oppressive, and what is unyielding — and Scripture denies the first of God and asserts the third of man.
biblical_def: Scripture uses hard to draw a line between God and man, and the line runs the opposite way from what we expect. Of God, the question is asked and answered: Is any thing too hard for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14). Jeremiah repeats it as a confession under siege: thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee (Jeremiah 32:17). Nothing is difficult to Him. But of man the word describes the heart, and there it is fatal. The warning stands over the whole letter to the Hebrews: Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness (Hebrews 3:8). A hard heart is not a strong one; it is one that no longer registers what it hears. Proverbs adds the practical verdict on the life built that way: the way of transgressors is hard (Proverbs 13:15) — sin is not the easy road, whatever it advertises. And the unprofitable servant supplies the corruption in its own words, excusing his idleness by an accusation: I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown (Matthew 25:24). He calls the master hard, and the master’s reply exposes the hardness as the servant’s own. What a man believes about God’s hardness usually describes his heart, not God’s character.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HARD as firm; solid; compact; not easily penetrated or separated; difficult to understand or accomplish; laborious; oppressive; severe; and, of persons, unfeeling, insensible, obdurate.
webster_full: HARD, a. [Sax. heard.] — Firm; solid; compact; not easily penetrated, or separated into parts; not soft. Difficult; not easy to the intellect. Laborious; fatiguing. Oppressive; rigorous; severe; as hard terms. Unfeeling; insensible; obdurate; as a hard heart.

Webster’s progression — from stone, to difficulty, to severity, to an unfeeling heart — is the biblical progression exactly. The last sense is a metaphor drawn from the first, and Ezekiel makes the figure explicit when God promises to take away the stony heart and give a heart of flesh.
scriptures: Genesis 18:14
Is any thing too hard for the LORD? At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son.
Jeremiah 32:17
Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee:
Hebrews 3:8
Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness:
Proverbs 13:15
Good understanding giveth favour: but the way of transgressors is hard.
Matthew 25:24
Then he which had received the one talent came and said, Lord, I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed:
corruption_summary: Hard is corrupted when the hardening of the heart is treated as something that merely happens to a man — a misfortune or a psychological injury — rather than an act for which Scripture holds him responsible and against which it issues a direct command.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 3:8 is an imperative addressed to the will: Harden not your hearts. It is not a description of a condition that overtakes people. The modern instinct is to explain hardness as the residue of what a person has suffered, and therefore to treat it as an injury to be tended rather than a sin to be repented of. Scripture is more merciful than that, because it is more honest. It grants that hardening happens gradually, in a wilderness, through repeated provocation — and it still commands against it and still holds men accountable for it. Where hardness is only ever explained, it is never repented of, and a man may be sympathized with all the way to the judgment. The command implies that grace is available to obey it.

The second corruption is the servant’s in Matthew 25:24, and it is remarkably common: the sinner attributes hardness to God and uses that attribution to justify doing nothing. I knew thee that thou art an hard man is offered as an excuse and functions as an accusation. Scripture’s answer is that no such hardness exists in God toward His people — He is the God for whom nothing is too hard and who gave His own Son — and that the charge reveals the accuser. This matters wherever the doctrines of grace are taught, because sovereign election is regularly caricatured as making God hard. The Reformed answer is the servant’s parable read straight: the man who calls his master hard has not looked at the master, and the God who hardened Pharaoh is the same God who asked Abraham, with a son in view, whether anything is too hard for the LORD.
roots_summary: The Hebrew keeps two distinct ideas apart that English merges. One root means too difficult, surpassing and is used of God’s ability; another means stiff, stubborn, severe and is used of man’s heart. The first is the same root that gives wonderful.
roots_lines: Hebrew pālā (H6381) — to be extraordinary, surpassing, beyond reach; the word behind too hard for the LORD (Genesis 18:14) and behind Wonderful in Isaiah 9:6.
Hebrew qāshāh (H7185) — to be hard, stiff, stubborn, severe; the verb of the hardened heart and the stiff neck.
Hebrew chāzaq (H2388) — to be strong, to strengthen; also used of hardening, as of Pharaoh’s heart, where strengthening in resolve is the hardening.
Hebrew lēb (H3820) — heart; the organ of will and understanding, and therefore the thing that hardens. Not the seat of emotion merely, but of decision.
usage: Is any thing too hard for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14) — the question is rhetorical, and Sarah heard it while laughing.
Harden not your hearts (Hebrews 3:8) is an imperative, which means hardening is a thing men do rather than a thing that merely happens.
The way of transgressors is hard (Proverbs 13:15): sin advertises ease and delivers difficulty.

etymology: From Old French tendre, from Latin tener, soft, delicate, young. Webster 1828: soft; easily impressed or broken; susceptible of the softer passions; compassionate. In the Authorized Version tender describes three things — a young plant, a compassionate God, and a heart that can still be broken by His word.
biblical_def: Tender in Scripture is not weakness; it is the capacity to be affected. Its highest use belongs to God: David appeals to the multitude of thy tender mercies (Psalm 51:1) at the point where he has no other appeal left, and Zacharias names the whole incarnation as its fruit — Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us (Luke 1:78). The Hebrew and Greek behind these phrases are visceral words, drawn from the inward parts, and they mean compassion that is felt rather than merely decided. The word then describes what God commends in a man. Josiah is told, Because thine heart was tender, and thou didst humble thyself before God, when thou heardest his words (2 Chronicles 34:27) — the exact opposite of the hardened heart, and the reason the judgment was deferred in his days. Paul makes it the church’s manner: be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you (Ephesians 4:32), where the pattern and the power are both God’s prior forgiveness. And Isaiah uses the word of the Messiah’s beginnings: he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground (Isaiah 53:2) — unimpressive, easily despised, and the strength of God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TENDER as soft; easily impressed, broken, bruised or injured; delicate; effeminate in constitution; also susceptible of the softer passions, as love, compassion, kindness; and careful not to injure.
webster_full: TENDER, a. [Fr. tendre; L. tener.] — Soft; easily impressed, broken, bruised or injured; not firm or hard; as tender plants; tender flesh. Susceptible of the softer passions, as love, pity, kindness; compassionate. Careful to save inviolate, or not to injure; as tender of reputation. Young and weak.

Webster’s first sense — easily impressed — is the doctrinal one. A tender heart is one that takes an impression from the word of God, which is exactly what Josiah’s did and exactly what a hardened heart cannot do. The word is about receptivity before it is about sentiment.
scriptures: Luke 1:78
Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us,
Psalm 51:1

To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came unto him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba. Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.
2 Chronicles 34:27

Because thine heart was tender, and thou didst humble thyself before God, when thou heardest his words against this place, and against the inhabitants thereof, and humbledst thyself before me, and didst rend thy clothes, and weep before me; I have even heard thee also, saith the LORD.
Ephesians 4:32
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
Isaiah 53:2
For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
corruption_summary: Tender is corrupted when receptivity to God’s word is replaced by mere sensitivity to feeling — so that a tender heart comes to mean one easily upset rather than one easily convicted — and when God’s tender mercy is set against His justice as though the two were rivals.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption substitutes emotional delicacy for the thing Scripture praises. Josiah’s heart was tender in a specific and demonstrable way: he heard the words of the law, understood that judgment was deserved, humbled himself, rent his clothes, and wept — and then he tore down the high places. Tenderness there is the capacity to be broken by the word and to act on it. A man may be highly sensitive, quick to distress, and entirely unmoved by Scripture; that is not tenderness in the biblical sense but its counterfeit, and it can coexist with a completely hardened conscience. The test is not how readily a heart is affected, but by what.

The second corruption sets God’s tenderness against His justice, so that tender mercy becomes an argument for expecting God to overlook sin, and eventually for denying that He will judge at all. But Psalm 51 is prayed by an adulterer and murderer who has just been confronted by a prophet, and it appeals to tender mercies precisely for the blotting out of transgressions — the mercy is aimed at guilt, not at its dismissal. Luke 1:78 locates that tender mercy in the visit of the dayspring from on high, which is to say in the incarnation of the One who would bear the judgment. Tenderness and justice meet at the cross rather than competing, and a tenderness that costs God nothing is not the tenderness the Bible describes.
roots_summary: Two word families supply tender. One is the language of the womb and the inward parts, used of God’s compassion; the other is the plain adjective for what is soft, young, and easily impressed, used of plants and of hearts.
roots_lines: Hebrew rachamim (H7356) — compassion, tender mercies; a plural noun built on the word for womb (Psalm 51:1).
Hebrew rācham (H7355) — to have compassion, to show deep mercy; the verb of the same family.
Greek splagchnon (G4698) — the inward parts, and by metonymy the seat of compassion; behind the tender mercy of our God (Luke 1:78).

Hebrew rak (H7390) — tender, soft, weak, gentle; used of Josiah’s heart (2 Chronicles 34:27) and of the tender plant of Isaiah 53:2. Greek eusplagchnos (G2155) is the New Testament’s tenderhearted (Ephesians 4:32).
usage: The multitude of thy tender mercies (Psalm 51:1) is what a guilty man appeals to when he has nothing else.
Josiah’s heart was tender (2 Chronicles 34:27) — he heard the word, humbled himself, wept, and then acted.
The Messiah grows as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground (Isaiah 53:2): unimpressive, and the arm of the LORD.
